title: Symphony No. 1 in C minor
hook: Years in the making, it climbs from pounding drums in the dark to a horn call over the mountains.

painting.title: The Lake of Thun
painting.pairingNote: A sunlit Swiss mountain lake under snowy peaks; the world of the alphorn call Brahms sent to Clara Schumann in 1868 and set at the heart of the finale.

facts: Brahms himself said the symphony took 21 years, from 1855 to 1876. He was haunted by Beethoven and destroyed or reworked many early attempts. Brahms’s friend Felix Otto Dessoff conducted the premiere in Karlsruhe on 4 November 1876. Brahms was 43.
The conductor Hans von Bülow called it “Beethoven’s Tenth”. The big tune of the finale reminded many of the “Ode to Joy”; Brahms is said to have replied: “any ass can see that”.
The horn call that lights up the finale goes back to September 1868, when Brahms sent it on a card to Clara Schumann: “Thus blew the shepherd’s horn today!”
Trombones play only in the finale, and first enter quietly with that horn call.
bigPicture.inOneLine: struggle (I), tenderness (II), a gentle interlude (III), darkness into light (IV).

movements.heading: Un poco sostenuto – Allegro
movements.summary: A slow introduction of enormous tension, then a fierce, driving [[sonata-form|sonata form]] movement. After all the struggle it ends, surprisingly, in a quiet C major.

mainIdeas.name: The introduction
mainIdeas.description: violins climb while the woodwinds fall, over a timpani pounding a single note.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a restless, strenuous melody in the violins, full of wide leaps.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a calm, warm tune in the oboe, clarinet and horn.

stops.hear: Timpani pound one note over and over; violins strain upwards while the woodwinds slide down
stops.happening: The introduction. The lines pull apart like a rope under strain

stops.hear: Quieter: plucked strings, a lonely oboe
A sharp chord, then the violins launch a tense, leaping theme
Strings and timpani tap out a short-short-short-long rhythm
stops.happening: An echo of the “fate” motto of Beethoven’s Fifth

stops.hear: The storm calms; oboe, clarinet and horn sing a gentle tune
The music turns away into distant keys, breaking up its themes
A low rumble in the basses, then rising arpeggios in the violins over brass
The first theme at full force
Plucked strings, slowing down

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Soft, broad chords
stops.happening: A calm close in C major

movements.heading: Andante sostenuto
movements.summary: A slow movement of great tenderness. Near the end a solo violin takes over the melody, like a voice singing alone.

stops.hear: Strings, with a bassoon, in a slowly rising melody
The oboe sings a long, song-like tune
A lilting, dotted rhythm in the strings
The oboe again, sadder, in C-sharp minor; then a clarinet
stops.happening: The mood clouds over, then brightens

stops.hear: The woodwinds bring back the opening theme
A solo violin, high and sweet, with soft horns
stops.happening: The oboe’s tune passes to the solo violin

stops.hear: Solo horn and solo violin together

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The violin solo is played by Michel Schwalbé.

movements.heading: Un poco allegretto e grazioso
movements.summary: Instead of a stormy [[scherzo|scherzo]], a light, graceful interlude: a clarinet tune, a lively middle section, and a quiet close.

stops.hear: A clarinet sings a calm, stepping tune over plucked cellos
Flute, clarinet and bassoon in a falling, dotted figure
Shorter, sharper phrases in the minor
The metre changes to a lilting 6/8; flute, oboe and bassoon share a cheerful tune
The clarinet tune returns, with echoes of the trio around it

stops.label: Last seconds
stops.hear: A soft, gently throbbing ending

movements.heading: Adagio – Più andante – Allegro non troppo, ma con brio
movements.tempo: Adagio – Più andante – Allegro non troppo, ma con brio
movements.summary: The longest and most dramatic movement. It begins in darkness, breaks into light with a horn call, sets off on a great striding tune, and ends in blazing C major.

stops.hear: Slow, dark descending notes in the strings; a sad hint of a tune
Plucked strings, faster and faster, tossed between high and low; then a timpani roll
stops.happening: Tension builds to a breaking point

stops.hear: A horn sings a broad call over shimmering strings; a flute answers
stops.happening: The alphorn theme, in C major

stops.hear: Trombones and bassoons in a soft, solemn [[chorale|chorale]]
stops.happening: The trombones, held back until the finale, lead a hymn

stops.hear: The violins begin a big, warm, striding tune
stops.happening: The main theme of the Allegro, often compared to the “Ode to Joy”

stops.hear: A falling figure in the low strings, gentler
The big tune again, then a stormy working-out
The horn call returns, at first troubled, then serene
Faster music, then the full orchestra sings the chorale at full volume
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]]: the solemn chorale, now in triumph

stops.label: Last bars
stops.hear: Hammered C major chords

notice: The finale’s main tune is not the horn call but the striding violin melody at ≈ 4:10. Brahms gives it to the strings quietly first; only later does the whole orchestra take it up.

threads.title: From C minor to C major
threads.body: The symphony moves from struggle to triumph, a path Beethoven’s Fifth had made famous.

threads.title: The shadow of Beethoven
threads.body: The fate rhythm in the first movement and the “Ode to Joy” likeness in the finale are both nods to the composer Brahms felt behind him.

threads.title: The horn call
threads.body: An alphorn melody, sent to Clara Schumann in 1868, becomes the turning point of the whole work.
